findings.title: Any admin-reader can pin itself and become an unremovable root; pinned keys are unrestricted and step 14 only forbids shrinking
findings.detail: Step 13 lets any head.pinned key author; step 14 lets a pinned author un-pin; step 15 exempts an author that is in the NEW record's pinned; step 14 forbids removing pinned entries but places no restriction on adding them. Sequence: head n has acl={A:7,B:7,C:1}, pinned={BK}. A (or whoever stole A's key) authors n+1 with pinned={BK,A}, acl={} (or {A:7}), dek_version+1 with fresh M, wraps={BK,A}. Step 13 ✓ (A ∈ admins(head)), 14 ✓ (head.pinned ⊆ pinned), 15 exempt (A ∈ pinned of the new record), 7 ✓ (A ∈ pinned). B and C are gone in one epoch; only BK (offline) can author now. n+2 by A: pinned={A} — allowed because A ∈ head.pinned — and BK is out for good: irrecoverable takeover from one admin key in two epochs; 'Lockout cannot happen as long as the backup key is pinned' is a policy nobody enforces. In server-recipient mode A can also un-pin OP: the server can no longer decrypt, every write-only identity is stranded and the service admin loses read — a unilateral mode flip. Even without n+2, A (or a second unregistered key K2 A controls) is a permanent recipient and author no other admin can remove (step 14 forbids non-pinned authors from shrinking pinned): a silent persistent backdoor that survives A's own removal from the ACL. Replicas verify and accept all of it.
findings.fix: Type pinned entries: pinned = [[id, role]] with role ∈ {backup, operational}. Only role=backup keys get steps 13/14/15 authority; role=operational is recipient-only. Any change to the pinned set (add or remove, any role) requires author ∈ backup(head.pinned). Step 15's exemption must read head.pinned's backup set, never the new record. Server and every replica are configured with the expected backup key id(s) and refuse any epoch — including epoch 1 — in which a configured backup id is not pinned. This also fixes the mode-flip and the K2 backdoor.

findings.title: Server-recipient mode pins the operational key, so a compromised server is a chain root; 'cannot forge ACL changes replicas accept' and 'service admin has no epoch authority' are false there, and Grant/RotateDek launder attribution
findings.detail: 12.4 pins the server's operational key OP in every epoch and 12.5 has the server author epochs with it for Grant/RotateDek/RemoveIdentity. A pinned author is exempt from steps 14 and 15 and may un-pin. Sequence: the server process (or anyone who compromised it) authors n+1 with acl={X:7} (attacker key), pinned={OP} (BK un-pinned, allowed since OP ∈ head.pinned), dek_version+1 with fresh M. Steps 13 ✓, 14 ✓, 15 exempt, 7 ✓. Every replica verifies and accepts: X is admin everywhere and the backup key is gone — strictly more than 'withholding', and exactly the forgery 12.4 says is now impossible. Second: a legacy Grant by group admin G is authored by OP, so the chain records 'the server did it' and G exists only in the unsigned, truncatable server audit log — the user's attribution goal is defeated for every client still using Grant/RotateDek. Third: a service admin keeps full implicit root through Grant/RotateDek/RemoveIdentity because the server signs whatever it asks; 12.1's 'no implicit epoch authority' holds only in E2E mode, which is not the recommended default for the existing bunker.
findings.fix: Give OP role=operational (recipient-only, see finding 1). If the server must author at all, restrict OP-authored epochs to exactly RemoveIdentity semantics, verifier-enforced: acl(new) ⊆ acl(head) entrywise (rows removed or bits cleared only), pinned unchanged, dek_version = head+1, and step 15 applies. Grant/RotateDek by group admins must be client-signed epochs even in server-recipient mode (server-side encryption is kept; server-side governance is not). Rewrite 12.4: in server-recipient mode a compromised server can kick and read, it cannot grant, pin or un-pin.

findings.title: Identity table and chain ACL are two unreconciled principal sources: in E2E mode RemoveIdentity is not a revocation on replicas, re-registration silently revives, and admins can enroll unregistered keys the operator cannot revoke
findings.detail: 12.4 E2E: RemoveIdentity 'removes the row (immediate transport denial) and marks affected groups rotation pending until an admin-reader submits the kicking epoch'; 12.5: replicas derive their ACL from the verified head. Sequence A: head acl={A:7,R:1}; service admin removes R. The chain still says R:1; apply_group_sync rule 1 (store.rs:1057) recreates R's identity row on every replica from the ACL, so R keeps reading through every replica — including the k8s operator that renders Secrets — not for sync lag but 'until some admin volunteers'. 'Rotation pending' is server-local and invisible to replicas. Sequence B: before any kicking epoch, a service admin registers the same endpoint id under a new name (AddIdentity accepts any unused endpoint id): R is instantly re-authorized on the authoritative node with its full chain perms (including admin) — no epoch, no signature, nothing attributable. Sequence C: admin A authors acl={A:7,K:1} where K was never registered — the verifier requires only decode_point. K is a recipient in the chain and authorized on replicas; RemoveIdentity cannot target it (no row); only a group admin or BK can ever kick it. Today RemoveIdentity is 'never blocked' and rotates every group in one transaction (remove_identity_with_rotations); the design regresses the operator's global-revocation power to 'ask an admin'.
findings.fix: (1) At SubmitEpoch the server rejects any acl or pinned id that is not a registered identity (configured pinned roles excepted). (2) AddIdentity refuses an endpoint id that still appears in any chain head's acl or pinned. (3) Sync carries an unsigned per-group `revoked: [endpoint_id]` list that replicas honour only in the deny direction (an unsigned denial can only reduce access, so a hostile server gains nothing beyond withholding); replicas subtract it from the effective ACL until an epoch removes the id. (4) In E2E mode, RemoveIdentity by a service admin who is not an admin-reader of an affected group returns a pending-rotation list, and ListGroups exposes 'rotation pending' so admins can act.

findings.title: Step 7 checks the new ACL, so an admin without read can grant itself read through a destructive rotation
findings.detail: Step 7: 'author ∈ readers(acl) ∪ pinned if dek_version changed or any recipient was added' — `acl` is the record's own. Sequence: head acl={A:7, M:4 (admin, no read), R:1}. M authors n+1: acl={A:7, M:7, R:1}, dek_version+1 with an M' it chooses, wraps to all three plus pinned (M knows M', so proof and dek_commit are valid), `reencrypted` = digest of ciphertext it produced under KDF(M') — garbage, since it never held the old DEK — and sig by M. Step 7: dek_version changed → author ∈ readers(new acl) ✓ (M just added itself); 12 ✓, 13 ✓, 15 ✓. Old data is destroyed (loud, attributable), but every future Put — server-recipient: the server encrypts under the new DEK; E2E: writers use head's DEK — is readable by M. The 'membership manager' role 12.1 explicitly carves out ('an admin without read may edit w/a bits') escalates to reader of all go-forward secrets. The proof cannot stop this because M' is the author's own; only the authorization check can, and it is self-satisfying.
findings.fix: Step 7 must test the previous epoch: whenever dek_version changes or recipients(new) ⊄ recipients(head), require author ∈ readers(head.acl) ∪ backup(head.pinned) (epoch 1: the record itself). Optionally also require author ∈ readers(new) so an author can verify its own commit.

findings.title: Removing a reader without bumping dek_version is accepted — a forward-secrecy regression versus today's revoke_read_and_rotate
findings.detail: Step 12 allows dek_version unchanged with any ACL as long as dek_commit is unchanged; nothing ties recipient removal to a generation bump (12.3 describes a kick as bumping, but the verifier does not require it). Sequence: head acl={A:7,R:1}, dek_version=k. A authors n+1: acl={A:7}, dek_version=k, same dek_commit, fresh r, wraps={A,BK}, reencrypted=0. Steps 3, 6, 12 ✓. R is off the ACL but still holds M, so every secret written from now on is under KDF(M,k) and R decrypts it from any DB copy, backup, replica mirror or captured sync stream. Today store::revoke_read_and_rotate makes this state unreachable; the design moves the rotation to client good behaviour, and a lazy or malicious client (or a race-winning quick 'kick' that skips re-encryption) silently voids the revocation guarantee of crypto-design.md §7.
findings.fix: Step 12: if recipients(head) ⊄ recipients(new) then dek_version == head.dek_version + 1 and reencrypted ≠ 0 are mandatory. Enforceable with no key. Bumping without removal (explicit rotate) stays allowed.

findings.title: Genesis pinned set is unchecked, and re-genesis, rollback and fork behaviour for replicas is unspecified
findings.detail: (a) 12.2: the server checks epoch 1 with steps 1–9, 13, 15 only; step 14 has no head. A creator can mint epoch 1 with pinned={} or pinned={K2}: BK is never a recipient, the operator can never recover the group, and 12.1's lockout guarantee is void from birth. (b) 12.5 says replicas 'pin hash(epoch 1)' but never says what a mismatch does. A compromised — or merely restored-from-backup — authoritative node presents a different epoch 1 under the same group name (the migration rule even lets the authoritative endpoint key author it). Accept = complete ACL forgery; reject = a legitimate group recreation under the same name wedges the replica forever. Groups are keyed by name on the wire. (c) Rollback: a server serving a prefix of the chain (authoritative restore) — store.rs:1090 today explicitly accepts rewinds as 'the local one is the stale copy' — reverts the replica's ACL, revives the kicked reader R on that replica and reinstates ciphertext under the old generation. (d) Fork: A and B each sign n+1 on the same prev (admin-kicks-admin race); the server commits A's, keeps B's bytes, and serves B's branch to replica R2. Two validly signed heads; R2 serves attacker B. 'Degrades to withholding' is too strong: the server can also choose which admin won.
findings.fix: Server enforces pinned(epoch 1) == configured policy set (and, per finding 1, backup pinned in every epoch). Replicas key mirrored groups by group_id bytes, record group_id → genesis hash, refuse a different genesis for a known group_id, and treat a new group_id under a known name as a new group needing operator acceptance. Replica head rule: the new head must be a strict descendant of the local head (the tail must link from local head_hash); prefixes and siblings are rejected, and an authoritative restore is an explicit `replica reset --group` operator action. Replicas expose (group_id, head_epoch, head_hash) so the operator can alarm on divergence, and the server audit-logs the hash of every rejected epoch so a fork served later is attributable to the server.

findings.title: SubmitEpoch's re-encrypted version set is not bound to the group's actual version set: a Put race strands versions, and the epoch path bypasses the write permission
findings.detail: 12.3: the server applies epoch + uploaded versions + pruning under a CAS on (group_id, head_epoch); step 9 only checks that `reencrypted` matches what was uploaded. (a) Race: writer W Puts (s,5) under dek k after admin A snapshotted the group for its k→k+1 epoch; Put does not bump head_epoch, so A's epoch commits without (s,5). (s,5) stays under generation k — a key the kicked reader holds — so the kick's forward protection fails for exactly the write that raced it, and the group is left with current versions under a 'pruned' generation. (b) Permission bypass: an admin-reader without the write bit uploads extra (name, version) rows, or omits some so they are pruned: it creates or deletes secrets through SubmitEpoch, which today needs PERM_WRITE. (c) Stale writer: in E2E mode a writer encrypts under k after the head moved to k+1; no rule says the server rejects a Put whose dek_version ≠ head.dek_version.
findings.fix: Inside the SubmitEpoch transaction: require the uploaded key set == the group's retained (name, version) set exactly, and allow only (dek_version, nonce, ciphertext) to change per row. Maintain a per-group write_seq bumped by every Put/Delete and include it in the CAS (the client echoes the seq it snapshotted). Reject any Put or uploaded version whose dek_version ≠ head.dek_version with VersionConflict-style feedback.

findings.title: Re-encryption lets any admin-reader rewrite historical plaintext under the original writer's created_by
findings.detail: 12.3 re-encrypts every retained version 'version numbers unchanged'; the `reencrypted` digest covers only (name, version, dek_version, nonce, SHA-256(new ciphertext)); created_by and created_at (secret_version columns stamped by the server from the transport identity) are preserved. Sequence: (s,3) created_by=alice. Admin A rotates and uploads (s,3) as the encryption of a different plaintext under the new DEK. Digest matches, epoch verifies, the row still says alice wrote it at the original time. The chain records only 'A re-encrypted at epoch n'. Today only an operator with SQLite write access could do this (crypto-design.md §2 lists it as out of scope for that reason); the design extends it to every admin-reader and silently breaks the brief's premise 'every reader can verify who produced the version' for all history.
findings.fix: Add a per-version plaintext commitment that survives re-encryption: content_commit = SHA-256('secret-bunker-epoch/1 content' ‖ 0x00 ‖ group ‖ name ‖ u64be(version) ‖ plaintext), computed by the server at Put in server-recipient mode or by the writer in E2E mode (ideally writer-signed with the endpoint key — the per-put signature the brief calls a natural extension). Put it in the AAD or in the `reencrypted` leaf and have readers check decrypted plaintext against it. At minimum include the old (dek_version, nonce, SHA-256(old ciphertext)) per leaf so a rewrite is auditable, and re-stamp created_by to the epoch author whenever the commitment changes.

findings.title: If the X25519-compat option is chosen, the backup key cannot author a recovery epoch — the recovery root has no authority
findings.detail: Open question 13.1 offers keeping the existing age backup key via the compat recipient mode (section 6). Section 7 requires the author to sign RFC 8032 pure Ed25519 verified with verify_strict under `author` = the pinned id A⁺ = MontgomeryPoint(u).to_edwards(0). The age identity holds a clamped scalar a with no RFC 8032 seed; a·B equals −A⁺ half the time, in which case no signature can verify under A⁺; and even when a·B = A⁺, neither Go `ed25519` nor `iroh::SecretKey` can sign from a raw scalar (dalek needs `hazmat::raw_sign` with a non-standard nonce). So a compat-pinned backup key is recipient-only: it can decrypt but cannot submit the recovery epoch that 12.1 and 12.4 rely on ('the only party that can always author an epoch'). In E2E mode, after an admin-kicks-admin takeover (or finding 1), the group is dead.
findings.fix: Make compat keys recipient-only by rule and require at least one Ed25519 role=backup pinned key in every epoch (verifier-enforced). If compat signing is really wanted, specify it fully (raw-scalar signing with a domain-separated deterministic nonce, and pin the Edwards encoding that actually equals a·B, not to_edwards(0)) with a Go implementation and its own golden vector — but recommend the key ceremony.

findings.title: GetEpochs disclosure and SubmitEpoch transport binding are unspecified
findings.detail: The epoch body carries the full roster (endpoint ids and perms) and every wrap. Today the roster is admin-gated on the client protocol and read-gated on sync; 12.5 gives GetEpochs no authorization rule. Readers need the chain to open their wrap, but a write-only identity in server-recipient mode does not. SubmitEpoch is likewise not bound to the transport identity, so any registered peer can commit an admin's signed-but-abandoned draft (a crashed client, or the losing side of a staged upload) as long as prev still matches.
findings.fix: GetEpochs requires an explicit ACL row on the group (uniform Denied otherwise, preserving the no-oracle rule); SubmitEpoch requires transport identity == author, or at least a registered identity, and is audited under both.

findings.title: The epoch body binds neither the group name nor pinned roles, so a verifier cannot tell which mode it is in
findings.detail: 12.4 says the mode is 'visible in every epoch's pinned list', but pinned entries are bare ids: a client cannot tell whether a given id is the operational key (server can read) or a second backup key. The group name is also outside the body; in server-recipient mode a compromised server holding M could present group P's chain (and P-keyed re-encrypted secrets, AAD recomputed under name S) under name S to a replica, extending P's readers to S. E2E mode is protected by the AAD only because the server lacks M.
findings.fix: Role-typed pinned entries (finding 1) and either the group name in epoch 1's body or a client-facing group_id so replicas and clients key groups by the chain's own identity rather than the server's label.

findings.title: A pinned author can leave a group permanently unmanageable (pinned={} and no admin)
findings.detail: Step 15 exempts a pinned author and step 14 lets it un-pin everything; step 3 only needs n ≥ 1. A recovery epoch with acl={X:1}, pinned={} verifies. 12.1 says a recovery epoch 'may temporarily have no admin', but nothing forces the temporary state to end, and once pinned is empty no key can ever author again.
findings.fix: Covered by finding 1's rule that a configured backup id must be pinned in every epoch; additionally require that an epoch authored by a pinned key either leaves an admin-reader in acl or leaves the backup set non-empty.

strengths: Recipient-set equality (step 3: wraps == readers ∪ pinned, no more, no less) plus strong Fiat-Shamir over every (A_i, c_i) makes hidden readers and wrap-set transplants impossible, and the argument that an admin without read cannot add, remove or re-randomise recipients without M or r is correct (CDH) — the proof actually enforces a governance rule, not just consistency.

Signing the exact received CBOR bytes, chaining on hash(body‖sig), and the server CAS on (group_id, head_epoch) close the classic replay/reorder/canonicalisation holes; a reader is never asked to open an unverified record.

Last-admin rule expressed as admins ∩ readers ≠ ∅ is the right unit (an admin without read cannot rotate), and the admin-kicks-admin default is argued honestly with its cost (only the backup key reverses a takeover).

The `reencrypted` digest under the author signature gives exactly the attribution the user asked for ('who last re-encrypted'), and section 9.3 is candid that the proof says nothing about M's correctness or the author's knowledge of it.

Two explicit deployment modes with different trust conclusions, and the admission that E2E mode turns RemoveIdentity into a two-phase operation, is better than pretending one mode fits both threat models.
verdict: The cryptographic core (torsion-strict Edwards ElGamal, strong-FS batched Chaum-Pedersen, signature over exact bytes, hash chain, server CAS) is sound, and the proof genuinely stops an admin-without-read from adding or removing recipients without M. The governance layer on top is not ready. Root cause: `pinned` conflates "mandatory recipient" with "unrestricted recovery authority", and step 14 only forbids shrinking it — so any admin-reader can pin itself and become an unremovable root, un-pin the backup key, or flip the deployment mode. In the recommended server-recipient mode the pinned operational key makes a compromised server exactly the chain-root the design claims it can no longer be, and legacy Grant/RotateDek launder attribution through the server key. The identity table and the chain ACL are two unreconciled principal sources, so in E2E mode RemoveIdentity is not a revocation on replicas and is undone by re-registration. Step 7 checks the new ACL and is self-satisfying; reader removal without a generation bump is accepted (a forward-secrecy regression versus today's revoke_read_and_rotate); genesis pinning, re-genesis, rollback and fork handling for replicas are unspecified; the re-encrypted version set is not bound to the group's real version set; and re-encryption lets any admin rewrite history under the original writer's created_by. Every one of these is fixable with verifier-enforceable, keyless rules (role-typed pinned entries with backup-only mutation rights, head-based step 7, forced rotation on recipient removal, replica head monotonicity plus genesis pinning by group_id, server-side set equality on SubmitEpoch, per-version plaintext commitments), but as written the design's own headline claims about lockout, server compromise and service-admin authority are false in its recommended configurations.
